stories.title_en: Luring a Sister-in-Law into Adultery to Cheat Them Out of Oil and Meat

paragraphs.en: Two sisters-in-law were sitting together when an oil seller passed by. The younger sister-in-law, Lady Shi, said, "We need oil in the house, but we have no silver to buy it." The elder sister-in-law, Lady Zuo, said, "Have him weigh out the oil first; paying him later will be soon enough." Lady Shi called him in and had two catties of oil weighed out. She said, "Our men aren't home; come back in two days for the silver." Two days later the oil seller returned. The younger sister-in-law said, "There is no silver—what shall we do?" The elder said, "Put him off for another three days." The younger used these words to send him away. After three more days the younger said, "You told me to have the oil weighed out first, and now there is still no silver. Lend me a little so I can pay him." The elder said, "If you are willing to do as I teach you, paying him back will be no trouble at all." The younger said, "I always follow your lead in everything—what should I give him to pay for it?" The elder said, "I see that young oil seller is handsome, and you are young and pretty. Be intimate with him once, and why would you need to pay for the oil?" The younger said, "I am afraid you might talk about it afterward." The elder said, "I am the one who taught you—how would I dare speak of it? I will step into the inner room to stay out of the way while you go and do it."

Shortly the oil seller arrived. Shi had no way to put him off. She forced a smile, came out to meet him, and said, "Twice I set a date to pay you, but I still can't raise the money. Better I return your silver." The oil seller saw her beaming, and lust rose in him: "There are people in your house—are you tricking me?" Shi said, "My husband’s in the fields; my mother-in-law is next door spinning hemp. There’s no one here, so I was teasing you." The oil seller was reassured and went into the room with her. Zuo heard the door bolted, slipped out, poured the oil from both half-baskets, filled both with water, then went back to listen at the door. The Aunt said, "Done—get up." The oil seller said, "Stay with me a bit." Zuo, hemp basket in hand, jumped out the main gate and deliberately shouted, "It’s not even noon—how is the field-worker back already?" The oil seller heard, hurriedly came out with his carrying-pole, and met her at the gate. Zuo asked, "Did my aunt pay you for the oil?" The oil seller quickly said, "Paid! Paid!" and carried it off to sell in the next village. Zuo knew he would come back, and waited at the main gate.

Near noon, the oil seller returned. Zuo said: "You're still here? My sister-in-law's brother came carrying buckets to fetch water. He saw a load of oil left in the house with no one around, except for some laughter coming from her room. Suspicious, he thought she was having an affair with the oil seller. He poured the oil into his buckets and filled the remaining space with water, then went home to tell his mother. Mother and son rushed over to catch them in the act. By the time they arrived, the oil carrier had already fled; they are still guessing about what happened. If they knew you were here, they would surely make you the target." The oil seller tried to leave. Zuo grabbed him: "I tipped you off; you ought to thank me." The oil seller replied: "Tomorrow I'll send you two jin of oil."

After several days, he indeed sent the oil. The sister-in-law changed her story, took it to her brother's wife, and said, "The other day I was standing at the gate when the oil seller passed by again. I teased him, saying, 'My sister-in-law says the silver for the oil hasn't been paid yet, yet you hurriedly claimed it was settled—there must be a reason. I'm waiting here to tell my brother.' Feeling guilty, he promised me two catties of oil, and now he has sent them. Since you traded your favors for this, I ought to share it with you." Her brother's wife replied, "In that half hour I got four catties of oil to use—thank you for showing me the way." The sister-in-law said, "If you listen to me, there are even better things to enjoy."

Soon someone called out selling meat. The two women called him in, each weighed out two jin, and told him to return for the silver. Three days later, the butcher came to collect. The elder woman weighed out silver of seven-tenths purity to pay him; the younger's portion was set for two more days. When the time came, the butcher arrived. The elder said, "Pay him with the same trick as before; I'll conveniently slip into the room." Shi came out, smiled at the butcher, and said, "I borrowed your meat and have no silver to pay. Today no one is home; better I pay you with my own flesh." The butcher saw how pretty she was, grinned, and said, "I only want a little bit of the meat around your waist." Shi replied, "The whole body is yours—why begrudge a little?" The butcher pulled her into the room and got down to business. The elder slipped out, moved the entire load of meat inside, and sat silently by the meat hampers.

The butcher finished his tryst with Shi and came out, asking: "Where has my meat gone?" Zuo replied, "Uncle took it to the village head." The butcher said, "How dare you steal my meat?" Zuo retorted, "You've got nerve! Uncle returned, saw the meat load here, noticed the bedroom door shut, heard you two laughing, realized you were with his wife, and ordered me to guard the door. I didn't want to eavesdrop on your antics, so I sat here. Just sit a moment; the man who stole your meat will be back soon." The butcher lifted the empty baskets and started to run. Zuo grabbed him: "Give me a meat knife as collateral." The butcher said, "Thanks for your help; tomorrow I'll send you two jin of meat." Zuo let go, and the butcher fled at full speed.

The younger complained: "It was you who taught me to do this. Now my husband knows—what then?" The elder said, "You shouldn't have exposed your master like that. As long as you're willing to eat the meat, covering this up is easy." The younger said, "What's the plan? Quick, tell me." The elder went in, dragged out one leg of meat, then another: "Will you eat the meat, or tell your husband?" The younger said, "You stole the meat! You shouldn't have scared me half to death." The elder replied, "I scared him away; if I hadn't scared him off, how would we have gotten his meat?"

The two sisters-in-law boiled the meat and shared a meal with wine. The younger said, "Truly: one day without shame brings three days of full bellies." The elder replied, "Not so—half an hour of pleasure buys a month of wine and meat." They laughed heartily, ate their fill, and ate the rest after it had been smoked.

A few days later, the butcher passed by. Lady Zuo came out and asked for two catties of meat on credit, and the butcher hurried on. Lady Zuo said, "My poor younger sister-in-law took a rough beating because of you the other day—you ought to give her two catties too." The butcher tossed over a cut of meat and said, "Please pass this along to her for me; I have no time to spare." Carrying the two strips of meat in hand, Lady Zuo went inside, told her younger sister-in-law the whole story, and brought the meat out for another merry feast. The younger sister-in-law said, "I may know how to keep a lover, but you are even better at playing the swindler!" Once the door to illicit affairs was opened, what followed was more than could ever be recorded.

Note: Aunt Shi was only a dull woman; Elder Zuo was a cunning, clever one. Had she been a man, she would have been a master of the game. Meeting such a clever woman, how would a fool not fall into her trap? So not only should men choose their company; women especially should keep company with good women.

stories.title_en: Climbing the Ashes: Cheating on the Mother-in-Law, Then Swindling Her

paragraphs.en: In the countryside there was a well-off old villager, granaries full of grain and beans, chickens and ducks in flocks. He was extremely rustic and coarse, with no sense of propriety. He married a farm girl as daughter-in-law, young and pretty, and thought of sleeping with her. He only feared the old lady’s strict control; household rules were tight, and for years he dared not act.

One day, the old mother-in-law was invited next door for a drink, and the old villager took the chance to make advances to his daughter-in-law. When she refused, he tried to force himself on her. Shouting and cursing, the young wife broke free and ran out. Her parents' home was only ten li away, so she ran there on foot to tell her mother. Her mother was a fierce, shrewish village woman, and she marched straight over with her daughter. Seeing that his daughter-in-law had run home to report him, the old villager hurriedly called his wife back, confessed the whole truth, and asked how they could deal with it. The old woman thought to herself: "The girl's father is a simple rustic and won't come; only her mother, that fierce shrew, is sure to arrive." Having already hit upon a scheme to trap her, she turned and congratulated her old man instead: "Congratulations! A stroke of good luck has arrived!" The old villager said, "What's done was a mistake—don't mock me. You've always been resourceful, and I listen to you in everything. Save me now, or our family will be ruined!" The old woman said, "Ruined? It'll cost you your life! Yet if I save you now, you'll only grow bolder. If you obey me and swear never to harbor such wild thoughts again, I'll not only save you, I'll treat you to a fine piece of luck besides." The old villager said, "I don't ask for any luck—just save me this once, and I'll never dare think a wicked thought again. If I do, may Heaven strike me and Earth destroy me!" The old woman said, "Since you've sworn, I'll spare you this time. Take four taels of silver in two ingots, and hide in the outer guest room underneath the big vat. When the girl's mother arrives, I'll have her bathe in that room. Once she finishes washing, crawl out from under the vat and press the two silver ingots into her hands. She'll surely clutch the silver and won't be able to push you away; then force yourself on her once, walk right out, and the whole matter will be settled." The old villager said, "If I violate her too, won't that prove I really did harass her daughter?" The old woman said, "Never you mind—leave the rest to me." The old villager did as told and hid beneath the vat.

Before long, the girl's mother arrived. The old woman came out with a welcoming smile and said, "Sorry to trouble your honored steps; we failed to prepare a sedan chair to meet you." The girl's mother immediately began cursing: "Your household has no decency! That old scoundrel of a father-in-law violated my daughter!" Feigning shock, the old woman cried, "Just now he fooled me by saying our daughter-in-law had secretly cooked herself a dish, and that she ran home because he beat and scolded her—how could he have done such a wicked thing? I'll have it out with that old dog to the death!" She cursed and railed at the top of her lungs, even more fiercely than her guest, leaving the girl's mother no room to get a word in. Then she said, "In a little while, you, I, my son, and my daughter-in-law—the four of us together—will seize him, beat him half to death, and pour nightsoil down his throat until he's unfit to show his face among men!" She ordered her daughter-in-law to slaughter plump chickens and ducks and lay out a lavish feast for her mother. After a round of loud cursing, they served tea and fruit, and the old woman said, "Walking in this heat makes one sticky; let us fetch water for you to bathe first, and then we can enjoy the midday meal in comfort." She ushered the girl's mother into the room to wash, while she herself went to the back kitchen to help her daughter-in-law warm the wine. Once the mother finished bathing, a man crawled out from beneath the vat, pressed two ingots of silver into her hands, threw his arms around her, and forced himself upon her. She cried out for her daughter and the old woman, but no one answered. The old villager said, "They are far off in the kitchen—how could they hear you?" Stripped for her bath, unable to break free, and reluctant to part with the two ingots of silver in her hands, she silently submitted to him. When it was over, the old villager said, "In-law, do not believe your daughter's tale. Our coming together today was also fated from a former life. I was hiding in here out of fear of you—who would have thought they would send you into this room to bathe, and that you and I would share this intimacy first? From now on, I will never harbor another thought toward your daughter." With that, he walked out.

The mother-in-law went into the kitchen, saw her daughter-in-law and the old maid still arranging the dishes, thinking they must not have heard her shouting, so at noon she drank and smiled at her ease, letting the matter of "climbing the ash" go unmentioned.

After the meal, she took her leave. The old lady repeatedly urged her to stay; the daughter also said, "I called you to be my host/sponsor; you only want to drink wine—how can you be such an old fool?" The mother-in-law replied, "As a woman, I cannot even make decisions for myself; how can I make them for you? Your father-in-law is no good, but your mother-in-law is virtuous. As long as the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law do not part ways, no evil will occur." Unable to keep her, the old lady gave generous gifts of food and fruit and happily saw her off. The scene of bitter wind and sudden rain suddenly transformed into bright breezes and fair sunshine—all thanks to this capable woman's mediation. She too was a great swindler.

Note: Women should not lightly visit their relatives by marriage. If a cunning woman colludes with her lover to set a trap, many are defiled—who would know? As with this old village woman tricking her mother-in-law: though it was a clever one-time ruse to settle a quarrel, she also knew that women’s hearts are as fickle as flowing water; they can be secretly lured by profit into a hidden snare for illicit affairs, yet dare not speak of it openly. Let future generations take warning.

stories.title_en: A Tenant’s Wife Sells Sex to Cheat the Landlord Out of His Land

paragraphs.en: In the countryside there was a tenant who owed the landlord three winters of grain rent, calculated at over five taels principal and interest. In winter the landlord came to collect. The tenant’s mother plotted with her son: "With this year’s, we owe three winters of grain; next year he’ll surely take the land back, and the whole family will have no hope. I see the landlord is a rich family’s son—he must be fond of romance. Better have the daughter-in-law trick him into a tryst, catch him in the act, and we can cheat the debt away." The tenant said, "That can work. Mother, speak to the daughter-in-law." The mother said, "One more thing: he must finish the deed before we catch him, so he’ll submit. If we catch him before it’s done, he’s the landlord—why would he accept being wronged? And it’ll be hard to make off with his silver." The tenant said, "That’s fine too." The mother then spoke to the daughter-in-law. The wife asked, "What does your son truly think?" The mother said, "I’ve spoken with my son. Let you complete the act, then catch him, so it can offset the rent." The three agreed.

Next day after the meal, the tenant pretended to go to his father-in-law’s house to borrow silver to repay the seed grain (miao) to the landlord. The mother also told her daughter-in-law: “When the master comes, there will be no dish; I’ll go to the upper village to beg for a jin of meat, then to my brother’s house to fetch a chicken. Whether the miao is repaid or not, we must host a meal for the master. You prepare a brazier for him to warm himself.” The master, standing outside, had already heard everything. After the two left, the wife brought out the brazier and fanned the fire. The master asked, “Where did your mother go?” The wife said, “To get dishes.” He asked again, “Where is your husband?” The wife said, “He went to my father-in-law’s to borrow silver to repay your miao; I don’t know if he’ll succeed.” The master said, “No need to borrow from your father-in-law; just borrow from you.” The wife said, “If I had silver, I would have sent it long ago.” The master said, “If you had slept with me last night, I would have settled the miao debt for you.” The wife said, “If sleeping can count as silver, come tonight and I’ll keep you company.” The master stood up: “Don’t wait for night; luckily there’s no one today—let’s play now. If your husband borrows the silver, I’ll secretly weigh out three qian for you to buy cloth; if there’s no silver, I’ll extend the deadline until next year.” The woman agreed; they went into the room. The tenant, watching from a hidden spot, quietly came out and waited outside the door. Hearing the two chatting happily inside, he was naturally agitated, wishing he could burst in immediately. After a long while, the master said, “Get up.” The wife said, “No hurry.” Knowing it was over, he shouted outside, “Who are you talking with?” and burst in. The two were too hurried to hide. The tenant shouted, “Ai! You thief—you’ve seduced my wife!” and dragged him off the bed to beat him. The wife hurriedly dressed, grabbed her husband’s hands: “You married me off; I’m not staying in your house!” The tenant said, “This hussy should be beaten to death too!” The three rolled in a heap; he couldn’t really beat them. Just then, the mother returned with meat and chicken: “What’s happening?” The tenant said, “The master seduced my wife; I caught them on the bed; I’ll beat these two to death.” The mother pointed at the master: “You’re a son of a good family; you shouldn’t do this. Better pay silver to my daughter-in-law to make up for the shame.” The master said, “I’ll write off three years’ worth of miao.” The tenant took the wife’s foot-binding, tied it around the master’s neck: “I won’t agree.” He went out, took a knife, and sharpened it: “I’ll kill him for sure!” The mother rushed out, snatched the knife: “He’s from an official family; silver and gold are plentiful—he has plenty to give. If you kill him, neither you nor I will live in peace.” She went back in and urged the master: “My son’s temper is bad; write him a land deed too.” The master said, “All right.” The mother fetched paper for him to write the deed. The tenant stood by and forced him to also write the adjoining fields, totaling twenty pu, priced at twenty taels. The master wrote that too. The mother conferred with her son again: “We only meant to write off the miao; unexpectedly we got twenty taels extra. Tonight you should stay away; let the daughter-in-law keep him company one night, so his heart submits and we can keep things safe.” The tenant said, “I’ve already recovered the cost of buying a wife; I’ll yield him one night.”

Late in the afternoon, they finally set out the wine. The tenant wished to invite others to join, but his mother said, "No; only I, an old woman, will keep him company." The three sat together, but the landlord merely asked for a meal and intended to return home. The mother then said, "My son was foolish just now; please do not take offense. I shall keep you company myself." She told her son to eat first and go to his maternal uncle’s house, pretending to borrow silver to help buy land. Once the son had left, the mother called the daughter-in-law out to keep the landlord company. The landlord said, "You mother and son have set a trap for me; tomorrow I will report this to the magistrate." The mother swore, "If I have tricked you, may I die this very day!" The daughter-in-law wept and said, "If you sue us, I will hang myself." Seeing her tears, the landlord reconsidered and thought it was no trap. He said, "I do not care whether there was a trap or not; sleep with me tonight, and I will let you go." The mother quickly agreed, "It is up to the daughter-in-law." The wife said, "I am determined to keep you company. If my husband speaks a word against it, then marry me." Fooled by this, the landlord stayed only one night and left; no further trouble arose.

Note: The tenant’s mother was extremely cunning. She had already set her trap, then made sure the illicit goods passed through her hands, and even demanded another night of company before the landlord finally felt satisfied. Otherwise, given the clear distinction between landlord and tenant, could mere empty words ever bind him? This tenant’s mother was a real master swindler; I recount this so future generations may know how to guard against such tricks.

stories.title_en: Three Women Make Off with Three Horses

paragraphs.en: On the Jingnan roads, people often kept horses to rent out to travelers, collecting daily profit. Three women traveling light met a horse-handler leading back three horses; each woman rented one. The youngest said, "Auntie who rides well, go first; we two who don't ride well will follow." Before ten li, the youngest called the handler to help her down, pretending to need to ease herself. He held her tightly as he lowered her, with a hint of taking liberties. She said, "You're trying to take advantage." He replied, "I wouldn't dare! I must hold tight so you don't fall." She said, "I see you know your business. I've had no husband for long; I'm not afraid of your holding." He said, "If you're not afraid, there's a small thatched hut ahead; how about another hug?" She said, "We have to hurry. Tonight we'll lodge at your house—how about that?" He said, "I don't have three beds." She said, "The two aunts can share a couch; I'll just stay by your bed." He said, "If you'll stay by my bed, I won't charge you horse rent." She said, "Comparing a person to a horse's price—you're trying to take advantage again." He said, "When both sides get a bargain, why wouldn't we do it?"

While they were making their secret arrangement, the woman's second-eldest uncle's wife ahead fell from her horse. The woman pointed at the groom: "Quick, go help my younger aunt." The groom walked forward but kept turning back: 'Don't try to trick me.' The woman said, "If the younger aunt gets badly hurt, she'll surely have to stop and rest on the road. Then our scheme is certain to succeed." The groom hurried off immediately.

The middle one fell and sat cross-legged on the road, saying: "I've hurt my foot and my leg too." The handler helped her mount, saying: "We must hurry." The middle one replied: "I'm injured; ahead we'll have to buy bruise plaster. We can only rest along the way—we can't make the destination. You go ahead and tell my eldest aunt to wait a little." By stalling twice like this, the front horse was already more than ten li ahead. The handler went forward to catch up, while the two women behind whipped their horses and raced back.

The handler couldn't catch the one ahead and thought: "Let her go on; I'll wait here for the two behind; they'll naturally wait to lodge together." He waited a long time; they didn't come. He thought again: "They must be buying plaster on the back road." He asked a passerby: "The two women on horses—where have they gotten to?" The passerby said, "The two women are racing like the wind; they're more than twenty li that way." The handler asked again: "Were they riding this way or going away?" The passerby said, "Going back down. Even if you hurry you won't catch them." The handler had no plan, hurried back to the original place, asked more people; all said, "The horses are already far." He chased back ten li; it was already dark. He asked travelers again; they said they hadn't seen the women or horses. The three horses had made off on two roads; he couldn't chase both front and back. The handler could only head home dejected.

Note: The clever getaway hinged entirely on the rear woman using a minor pretext to talk privately with the groom, confusing his mind and wasting his time; then the middle woman fell from her horse, making him suspect she truly couldn't ride, wasting even more time, while the front horse got away steadily. Thus they lured him to chase ahead—how could he catch up? The two behind raced back; he only thought the injured one was slow, never guessing they were racing the other way! But the groom was too foolish: who, meeting halfway, would immediately promise to let you stay? What charm did the groom possess that women would cling to him? Words too sweet hide poison. From the sweet talk itself, you know it's a swindle. When women possess such mastery, how can the world not be full of demons?

stories.title_en: A Nun Scatters Prayer Beads to Lure a Woman into an Illicit Affair

paragraphs.en: Bai Jian's wife, née Xiang, was very attractive. Jian loved wine and paid little attention to his wife. On business for Commander Wang, he was sent to the capital. While at home, Wife Xiang ran a paper-offering shop and often sent her maid Lanxiang to collect money and handle sales. With her husband gone for a long time, Xiang sometimes came out of the shop to gaze at passersby. Ning Chaoxian saw her, admired her beauty, and stared; Xiang did not avoid him. Chaoxian returned home and plotted with his close friend Cao Zhigao to lure this woman. Cao said, "To trick a woman, you need a woman working inside to make it easy. As the old saying goes: a mountain thief fights a mountain thief, a water pirate catches a water pirate. Nun Miaozhen of Fahua Convent often visits various households; go ask her, and the matter will be easy." Chaoxian was delighted, went to Fahua Convent, met Miaozhen, gave her two taels, and asked her to make contact with Bai Jian's wife in the paper-offering shop; if successful, there would be further heavy thanks. The nun said, "Not hard; come back in three days for a reply." Ning urged her repeatedly before leaving.

The nun cut the string of the prayer beads in her hand and twisted them tight. She paced back and forth several times in front of Bai Jian's shop but found no sign of Xiang, so she returned empty-handed. The next day she went again and saw Xiang sitting in the shop. Deliberately, the nun scattered the broken-string beads all over the ground; many rolled into the mud. She bent down to gather them from everywhere. Seeing this, Xiang called her inside, gave her water to wash, and the nun cleaned her hands thoroughly. The nun bowed repeatedly to thank her before departing.

The next day, the nun bought four items—cakes, fruit, pastries, and noodles—and sent someone to Xiang's house to express gratitude. Xiang was pleased and invited the nun over for a vegetarian meal with wine. At the table, Xiang asked, "At what age did you leave home?" The nun replied, "Midway through my life." Xiang asked, "Why?" The nun said, "I married a man who loved gambling and drinking, always out all day; having a husband was no different from having none, so I vowed to enter the convent." Xiang sighed, "Better not to marry than to marry such a man." Seeing she had moved her, the nun asked, "Why does Madam sigh?" Xiang replied, "My plight is much like yours. I married a man who only cares for drinking and never wants his wife; we don't even meet happily a few times a year. Now he has been sent far away on an official mission; it's as if I have no husband at all." Knowing the woman harbored wifely loneliness, the nun seized the moment: "Many men are wicked at heart. But Ning Chaoxian, whose temple is right before mine, loved his wife as his own life. Alas, she lacked fortune and died. Now he asks me to find him a new wife; any woman who meets him would truly be happy every single day." Xiang heard this but said nothing. The nun dared not press further; after the meal, she departed.

On the third day, Chaoxian dressed up and came to the convent for a reply. Miaozhen said, "Nine-tenths done. Women who get along with their husbands are very hard to stir. Yesterday Xiang invited me; I learned she resents her husband; and she’s been apart from him a long time; given a chance, she’s within grasp. Now I need silver; I’ll prepare a rich feast, invite her, pour good wine till she’s drunk; she’ll sleep in my bed; you unfasten her garments and slowly proceed, do as you please. But when she wakes, have bracelets, bangles, hairpins, and earrings ready to give her, to buy her heart, so you can maintain a long affair." Ning bowed: "If so, I won’t forget this in life or death. Here’s five more taels; quickly make the feast and invite her."

Miaozhen sent people to buy fine food and wine, had a cook prepare a rich and clean feast, first sending someone to invite, then going herself to fetch her. Xiang was delighted and came with Lanxiang in a sedan. Seeing the feast so lavish, she asked, "Who else did you invite?" Miaozhen replied, "Only Madam; no other guest." Xiang said, "For one person you needn't spend so much; how can we eat that much?" Miaozhen said, "I have no blood kin; I am grateful that Madam is a kindred spirit; I wish to become sisters, a true confidante." Xiang laughed, "You and I are confidantes, yet we cannot satisfy each other's needs." After a few cups, she asked, "This wine is fragrant and sweet; it must be expensive." The nun said, "Master Ning sent it the other day; I don't know its price." She urged her to drink more. Xiang said, "It's sweet and goes down easily, but I fear I'll get drunk quickly." The nun said, "If you get drunk, sleep a while in my room; head home after you wake, no rush. I don't know Madam's capacity—how much before you're drunk?" Xiang said, "At night if I can't sleep, I often drink a bottle. If I don't drink, how can I sleep?" The nun said, "If your husband were at home, just one cup from him would make you sleepy." Xiang said, "Let me tell you a truth between confidantes: even when drunk, I wake by midnight. My husband at home only greedily drinks and never wants to perform his duty. When I wake, it's unbearable—how can that quench my thirst?" Miaozhen said, "So having a husband is like having none. Daytime I can still endure; only nights I cannot; I only resent not planting merit in a past life." Xiang said, "Exactly so. Today I must get very drunk, hoping for one night of forgetting." Soon she collapsed drunk. Miaozhen sent Lanxiang home first to watch the house, then Xiang slept a while on the nun's bed.

While Lady Xiang was fast asleep, Chaoxian came in and undid her sash and clothes. She lay there like one dead, yet warm to the touch; he took his pleasure of her as he pleased, finding it utterly delightful. After a brief rest, he had his way a second time, and still she did not wake. Chaoxian held her tightly in both arms and slept until midnight. When she finally awoke, her clothes had already been taken off. Feeling a man lying beside her, a pleasant ease at her waist, and her whole body relaxed and refreshed, she whispered, "Who are you?" Chaoxian replied, "My darling, how long I have longed for you! Today I finally managed to steal two trysts with you—tomorrow you must be good to me again." Lady Xiang said, "Now that your scheme has succeeded, you must never let outsiders know." Chaoxian said, "Only the nun knows; who else could possibly find out?"

They slept until faint dawn; Xiang rose. Chaoxian gave her bracelets and embraced her, kissing her deeply. Still full of passion, they engaged once more, then went out hand in hand. Miaozhen was already waiting, unable to hold back her laughter, saying, "Good wine!" Xiang replied, "Good scheme!" Chaoxian declared, "What a perfect union!" Miaozhen asked, "Since it's so good, how will you thank me?" She hugged Chaoxian tightly: "My legs ache from all this work; be good with me as my reward." Chaoxian said, "I'm spent; I won't forget to thank you tonight." Xiang added, "From tonight on, we'll owe you every single night." Chaoxian remarked, "Our meetings can last long; our thanks can too." From then on, he frequently visited Xiang, entirely due to this seduction by the nun.

Note: Even a chaste woman, if led by a wanton woman, will enter into evil. A woman’s guarding her person is only knowing shame, only fearing people will know. Once she’s lost herself, shame is gone—what won’t she do? So households should be careful with nuns, matchmakers, and the like; don’t let them come and go. This is the right way to stop trouble at the start.
